title: HTML Forms
summary: Collect user input with form, label, input, textarea, select and button; understand name attributes, GET versus POST and what happens when a form is submitted.
introduction: Forms are how users talk back to a website: searching, logging in, ordering, commenting. An HTML form groups fields, labels them, and sends their values to a server when submitted. This lesson builds a complete contact form and explains the parts that beginners most often get wrong: labels that are not connected to fields, missing name attributes, and the difference between GET and POST.
learningObjectives: Build a form with text fields, a text area, a drop-down and buttons
Connect every field to a label and give it a name
Explain how submitted data travels and when to use GET or POST

blocks.text: `<form>` wraps the fields. `action` is the URL that receives the data and `method` is how it is sent. When the user presses the submit button, the browser collects every field that has a `name` and sends `name=value` pairs to the action URL.

blocks.code:
<form action="/subscribe" method="post">
  <label for="email">Email address</label>
  <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required>
  <button type="submit">Subscribe</button>
</form>

blocks.content: <form action="/subscribe" method="post"><label for="email">Email address</label> <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required> <button type="submit">Subscribe</button></form>

blocks.text: Two attributes are easy to forget and both matter. The label's `for` must equal the field's `id`; that connection lets screen readers announce the label and lets users click the label to focus the field. The `name` is the key under which the value is sent; a field without a `name` is silently left out of the submission.

blocks.title: Two silent bugs
blocks.text: A `<label>` without a matching `for`/`id` pair is not connected to anything, and an `<input>` without `name` never reaches the server. Neither produces an error message; you only notice when data goes missing.
You can also wrap the field inside the label, which connects them without ids:

blocks.text: With `method="get"` the values are appended to the URL as a query string (`/search?q=html&page=2`). That is right for searches and filters: the result can be bookmarked and shared. With `method="post"` the values travel in the request body, which is right for anything that changes data (sign-ups, orders, messages) or contains private information.

blocks.code:
<form action="/search" method="get">
  <label for="q">Search</label>
  <input type="search" id="q" name="q" placeholder="e.g. tables">
  <button type="submit">Go</button>
</form>

blocks.content: <form action="/search" method="get"><label for="q">Search</label> <input type="search" id="q" name="q" placeholder="e.g. tables"> <button type="submit">Go</button></form>

blocks.text: Submitting that form with "tables" typed in navigates to `/search?q=tables`. Try it on any site with a search box: the URL tells you the form used GET.

HTML only sends the data. Something on the server, written in [Node.js](/tutorials/nodejs), [Python](/tutorials/python), [PHP](/tutorials/php) or another language, reads the `name=value` pairs and stores them, emails them or replies with a new page. Without a server, submitting a form just reloads the page with the values in the URL.

blocks.title: Required fields
blocks.text: The `required` attribute stops the browser from submitting an empty field and shows a built-in message. It is a convenience for users, not security: anyone can bypass it, so the server must validate again. The next lesson covers validation attributes in detail.

seo.title: HTML Forms – form, label, input, select, textarea and Submission
seo.description: Learn HTML forms: the form element, labels connected to fields, name attributes, select and textarea, fieldset and legend, and the difference between GET and POST.
